objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain VOR, DME, NDB and GPS navigation, VFR radar services, the transponder and ADS-B at commercial-pilot depth, and teach a learner to navigate with them as a thinking pilot who cross-checks, manages the automation and talks to ATC correctly, instead of a button-pusher who follows a magenta line.
why: Glass panels, GPS and autopilots make navigation easy until something quietly goes wrong, and the FAA warns that humans are poor monitors of reliable automation and that pilots can drift into being a passenger in command [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. As the instructor you decide whether a learner understands the systems or only memorizes key presses. This lesson gives you the content, the traps the sources name, and teaching methods from the Aviation Instructor's Handbook to build real navigators.

warmup: Think first: your new learner, a private pilot, flies beautifully with the GPS and autopilot. You pull the GPS display's circuit breaker in your head and ask, 'Which way is the VOR from us, and which radial are we on?' The learner turns the OBS until the needle centers, reads the number, and then points the wrong way. What level of learning is this, which FAA warnings about automation does it illustrate, and how would you build this pilot into a navigator rather than a button-pusher?

key_terms.def: A line of magnetic bearing extending outward from a VOR station, numbered from 001 through 360 [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].
Shows whether the selected course, if intercepted and flown, takes the aircraft to or from the station. It does not show which way the nose is pointing [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
With the OBS set to the reciprocal of the intended course, the needle deflects away from the course and the pilot must turn away from it to correct [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
The straight-line distance DME measures from the aircraft to the station, so altitude is included; it is not horizontal distance [[33:72|AIM 1-1-7]].

Receiver autonomous integrity monitoring: the receiver's check that satellite signals meet the integrity requirement for the phase of flight. It needs 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]].
What all commissioned radar facilities give VFR aircraft: safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring when workload permits, and sequencing where established [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]].

A controller's alert that an aircraft is, in the controller's judgment, in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft; the pilot alone decides what action to take [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]].
Automatic pressure altitude reporting that replies to Mode C interrogations with pressure altitude in 100-foot increments [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215]].
Out is the aircraft's transmission of its GNSS-derived position and other data; In is the receipt of that information by an aircraft [[33:300|AIM 4-5-7]] [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].
Broadcast of ATC-derived traffic to ADS-B equipped aircraft; advisory only, and it shows only transponder-equipped aircraft [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8]] [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8]].
The demonstrated ability to control and navigate an aircraft by means of its automated systems, including knowing when to use them and when not to [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].
The lowest level of learning: the ability to repeat something without understanding or being able to apply it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]].

chunks.title: The CFI standard and the real goal

body.p: This Task asks you to understand navigation systems and radar services, apply that knowledge, manage the risks, demonstrate the skills and provide effective instruction (ACS AI.II.H). For each skill element the applicant demonstrates and simultaneously explains, so expect to talk while you fly. The ACS note tells the evaluator to use the manufacturer's equipment supplements for limits and procedures (ACS AI.II.H).

body.p: The deeper goal is a learner who navigates, not one who operates a box. The PHAK tells beginning pilots to use radio navigation to supplement pilotage, because visual navigation protects against disorientation if a radio fails [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. It also reminds us that only the pilot can navigate the aircraft; GPS is just one tool [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]. The AIM says VFR pilots should integrate GPS with other electronic navigation, pilotage and dead reckoning [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

callout.text: You cannot teach equipment you do not know. The AIH says a flight instructor must be thoroughly familiar with the functions and proper use of all avionics used for training, especially with the wide variety of GPS and glass displays [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

check.q: What does the PHAK say beginning pilots should do with radio navigation equipment?
check.a: Use it to supplement navigation by pilotage, which safeguards against disorientation if a radio fails [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

body.p: A button-pusher is a learner stuck at the rote level. Rote is the ability to repeat something without understanding or being able to apply it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Above it come understanding, application and correlation, and correlation, associating what was learned with other blocks of learning, should be the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

The AIH warns that application is the level at which instructors are too often willing to stop, and that moving on at that point is piecemeal instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. In navigation, a learner at application can track a radial; a learner at correlation notices that the VOR picture and the moving map disagree and knows what that means.

bullets: Teach the concept before the knobs. The PHAK says learning knob-and-dial procedures is not enough; learning how the system works gives better memory for procedures and lets a pilot solve problems not seen before [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

Teach stop, look and read. New pilots often fixate on knobs and try to memorize every sequence; reading before pushing saves trouble [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. The AIH gives the same strategy as stop, look and analyze [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

Use the right aids. Simulation software and manuals on the specific system are of great value to both instructor and learner [[25:22|AIH 1-18]], and most GPS receivers have a built-in simulator mode [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
Build blocks. When a skill relates to something already learned, known to unknown works; when several skills are taught together, simple to complex works [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Grade progressively. The AIH example: automation management is a describe item on flight one, a practice item by flight three and a manage-decide item by flight five [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

callout.text: Application: test for understanding with questions the box cannot answer for the learner, such as 'Which side of the station are we on?', 'What will the needle do if we keep this heading?' or 'What would you do if the map froze now?'. The AIH says the instructor can check situational awareness by asking where the aircraft is relative to references on the chart [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

check.q: Which level of learning does the AIH say should be the objective of aviation instruction?
check.a: Correlation: associating what has been learned, understood and applied with other blocks of learning [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

chunks.title: Ground-based navigation: identify, orient, find the course

body.p: VORs transmit between 108.0 and 117.95 MHz, so they are line of sight and range grows with altitude; at 1,000 ft AGL reception is generally about 40 to 45 miles [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. A radial is a magnetic bearing outward from the station [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

head: K1 item
What to teach
rows: Identification

The only positive identification is the Morse code or a recorded voice ending in the word 'VOR'. Never rely on an FSS or approach voice on the frequency [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]] [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]. If the receiver decodes the identifier you need not listen; if it only shows the expected identifier from its database, match it to the audio [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]].
Orientation

The VOR does not account for heading; it gives the same indications whichever way the nose points. Center the needle with FROM and the index shows the radial you are on [[23:254|IFH 9-11]] [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
Course determination
Set the desired course with the OBS. With TO showing, the course under the index leads to the station; with FROM, away from it [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]].
Equipment

CDI: full deflection means 12 degrees or more off course, the edge of the center circle is 2 degrees, each dot adds 2 [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. HSI: combines the heading indicator and CDI for a picture of position and direction [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. RMI: the pointer shows the course to the selected navaid with no course to set [[1:412|PHAK 16-25]]. DME: slant range up to 199 NM, accurate to 1/2 mile or 3 percent, whichever is greater [[33:72|AIM 1-1-7]]. ADF/NDB: needle points to the station; LF and MF signals are not line of sight [[1:416|PHAK 16-29]].

body.p: In the figure both airplanes have 180 set and a centered needle. The TO airplane is on the 360 radial and the FROM airplane on the 180 radial, whatever their headings [[23:254|IFH 9-11]] [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. This is the single most useful picture to teach orientation.

callout.text: The IFH lists turning in the wrong direction during orientation as a typical error, common until the pilot visualizes position rather than heading [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Make the learner say the position first ('south of the station, on the 180 radial') before any turn.

Teach the NDB's weak spot with the VOR's strength: ADF receivers have no flag, so the pilot must keep monitoring the NDB identifier; noisy identification usually comes with an erratic needle [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]].

check.q: A learner's receiver shows the identifier 'ABC' from its database but does not decode the signal. Is the station identified?
check.a: No. With that kind of equipment the displayed identifier only aids verification; the pilot must still match it to the audio Morse code [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]].

head: K1 item
What to teach
rows: Tests

VOT: center the needle and the OBS reads 0 with FROM or 180 with TO; an RMI shows 180 [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. Sensitivity: moving the needle from center to the last dot should take no more than 10 or 12 degrees each side [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. A receiver whose gain or modulation circuit is wearing out can pass near the VOT and be out of tolerance far away, so yearly calibration is recommended [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].
Regulations

For IFR using VORs: maintained under an approved procedure, or operationally checked within the preceding 30 days. Limits: 4 degrees with a test signal or designated ground checkpoint, 6 degrees airborne or over an airway ground point, 4 degrees between dual receivers [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171]]. The person checking enters date, place, bearing error and signs the log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171]]. For VFR there is no required tolerance; the PHAK suggests the IFR limits as a guide [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].
Interference

Some propeller RPM settings swing the CDI as much as 6 degrees each way; a small RPM change usually smooths it [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]. NDBs suffer from lightning and precipitation static and from distant stations at night [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]]. Transmitting on a combined NAV/COM can flicker the TO/FROM like station passage [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Report interference such as a hum or tone on the identifier [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].
Appropriate use of navigation data

Disregard any indication from a navaid NOTAMed unusable, however good it looks [[33:68|AIM 1-1-1]]. Disregard distance from automatically selected DME when the VOR has no DME [[33:73|AIM 1-1-7]]. The standard service volume does not protect against terrain blockage, and the cone above the station is generally unusable [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]].
Signal integrity

A flag means the signal is too weak, for example too far or too low [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]]. During maintenance the identifier is removed or the station sends T-E-S-T, a warning not to use it [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. One DME identifier about every 30 seconds with no VOR identifier means the DME is working and the VOR may not be [[33:72|AIM 1-1-7]] [[33:73|AIM 1-1-7]].

callout.text: Before you use any navaid: Tune, Identify, Flag clear, then Set the course. Say it out loud every time until the learner says it first.
Apply no correction other than the manufacturer's correction card when making VOR receiver checks [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

Application: make the first VOT or ground checkpoint check a demonstration on the ramp, then have the learner do the next one and write the log entry. It turns a rule into a habit and costs no flight time.

check.q: On a VOR you hear a single coded identifier about every 30 seconds and nothing else. What does it tell you?
check.a: The DME is operating; the VOR may not be [[33:72|AIM 1-1-7]] [[33:73|AIM 1-1-7]].

chunks.title: GPS: equipment, rules, databases and RAIM

body.p: The 24-satellite constellation is designed so at least five satellites are always visible, and a receiver needs four for a three-dimensional position [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]]. RAIM checks the integrity of the signals for the phase of flight; without RAIM the pilot has no assurance of position integrity, and a bad satellite can take up to two hours for the control segment to catch [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]].

head: K2 item
What to teach
rows: RAIM

Detect a fault: 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding. Detect and exclude (FDE): 6, or 5 plus baro-aiding. Enter the altimeter setting for baro-aiding; never use GPS altitude [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]]. Two message types: not enough satellites (integrity unknown), or a detected error too large for the phase of flight [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].
Equipment

VFR panel-mount and hand-held receivers have no RAIM alerting, so cross-check systematically and be suspicious when positions disagree [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. VFR antennas are placed for convenience, and a suction-cup antenna can lose satellites behind the structure [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. No design standard of accuracy or integrity applies to a VFR receiver [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].
Regulations and approvals

IFR GPS must meet TSO-C129, C196, C145 or C146 and be installed per AC 20-138; VFR and hand-held units are not authorized for IFR navigation [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. A hand-held needs no approval, but a mounting bracket or external antenna is a modification that does [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]].
Authorized use of databases

Databases must be current for IFR and should be updated for all other operations, but VFR has no requirement. Do not use a moving map with an outdated database around critical airspace, and verify waypoints with current charts [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. For IFR approaches, the procedure must be retrieved by name from the current database, never built from manually entered waypoints [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

bullets: VFR waypoints: five letters beginning with VP, not pronounceable and not for ATC use; load them on the ground and avoid programming routes or waypoint chains once airborne [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].
Mountain pass entry points are only for planning; flying from VFR waypoint to VFR waypoint does not create a path through the pass [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].
WAAS-only airplanes under part 91 need not carry VOR avionics, so prudent planning should consider a GPS outage [[33:70|AIM 1-1-3]].

callout.text: The PHAK says many pilots have flown into airspace they were trying to avoid by using an outdated database, and that a current database is needed to locate a named waypoint correctly [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]].

check.q: Your learner's VFR panel GPS shows a smooth, steady position. Why is that not proof the position is right?
check.a: VFR panel-mount and hand-held receivers have no RAIM alerting, so a bad position may give no warning; cross-check with other navigation [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

chunks.title: Teaching intercepts, tracking and position fixing

body.p: Orient first, then intercept. The IFH steps: find the difference between the radial to intercept and the radial you are on, double it for the intercept angle (not less than 20 or more than 90 degrees), set the OBS, turn to the intercept heading, hold it until the CDI centers, and lead the turn onto the course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. The PHAK adds that the intercept angle must be greater than the degrees off course but should not exceed 90 [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]].

bullets: Distance changes the picture: each radial is 1 NM wide at 60 NM, 2 NM at 120 NM and 1/2 NM at 30 NM, so the rate of intercept depends on distance from the station [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]].
Tracking: if the needle moves, correct toward it, starting with about 20 degrees; when it recenters, take out half the correction [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
Fly TO with TO and FROM with FROM, or the needle reverses [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]. Small fluctuations: wait a moment before changing heading [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]].
Just turning toward the needle produces overshoots and S-turns; that is homing, not tracking [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]].

Position (S2): one VOR gives a line; a second navaid fixes the point on it [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. A radial plus DME locates you precisely on that radial [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]]. GPS gives distance and track to the next active waypoint, not to a navaid [[33:99|AIM 1-1-17]].

Time and distance without DME: with an RMI, seconds for a 10 degree bearing change divided by 10 gives minutes to the station, and minutes times NM per minute gives distance [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]] [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]. Results are only approximate [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]].

body.p: How to teach it. Brief the intercept on the ground with a sketch of the station, the radial you are on and the one you want. In flight use telling-and-doing: you demonstrate while explaining, in the same sequence you briefed, because learners imitate the instructor [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Then the learner tells and you fly, which frees the learner to organize the steps and lets you check understanding before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: before the learner touches the OBS, ask 'Where are we, and where is the course?' If the answer is a heading, not a position, stop and draw it. The IFH also lists failure to parallel the desired radial as an error that makes intercepts confusing [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

check.q: Using the IFH method, you are on the 300 radial and want to intercept the 315 radial outbound. What intercept angle do you use?
check.a: The difference is 15 degrees; doubled, 30 degrees, within the 20 to 90 degree limits [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

head: System
What passage looks like
rows: VOR with CDI

The needle fluctuates, then settles, and TO changes to FROM. Passing to one side, the needle swings toward the station side as the flag changes [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]. Rapid or fluctuating movement means passage is near [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
Why it swings
A zone of confusion above the station, where the signal is inadequate and constantly changing [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
RMI
The pointer moves rapidly, or several corrections are needed to keep it on the wingtip [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]].
DME
Over the station it still shows your height as distance: about 1.0 NM at 6,076 ft AGL [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]] [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]].
GPS fly-by waypoint
The receiver starts the turn before the waypoint and rolls out on the next course [[33:110|AIM 1-2-1]].
GPS fly-over waypoint
The aircraft must cross the point before the turn starts; a missed approach waypoint is always fly-over [[33:110|AIM 1-2-1]] [[33:99|AIM 1-1-17]].

body.p: False passage. In mountains a brief needle oscillation can look like approaching the station, so use the TO/FROM indicator for positive passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]. Transmitting on a NAV/COM without an ON/OFF flag can make the TO/FROM flicker; read the whole receiver and ignore readings taken while transmitting [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. A GPS can sequence to the next waypoint while you are vectored or deviating, just from passing near a waypoint; the non-sequencing mode prevents that [[33:99|AIM 1-1-17]].

callout.text: S4 asks the learner to recognize and describe passage. Have the learner call it every time: 'Needle swinging, flag FROM, station passage, turning to 095, OBS 095.' Callouts, even single pilot, maintain situational awareness [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

check.q: Your learner, en route on a VOR radial, sees the needle flick and the flag flash just as you key the mic. Is that station passage?
check.a: Not necessarily. Transmitting on a combined NAV/COM can mimic passage; read the whole receiver and disregard readings taken while transmitting [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

chunks.title: Managing the automation: anticipate, act, verify

body.p: Automation takes the pilot's input, works out a solution and acts without continuous input; used properly it reduces workload and frees attention for the flight path [[30:50|RMH 7-1]]. It can also create more work and confusion, lull pilots into complacency and erode hand-flying skill [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

bullets: Anticipate: understand the system well enough to know what should happen before pushing a button. Act: make the entry. Verify: make sure the aircraft or avionics does what you expected [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

Know at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify that armed modes such as navigation tracking or altitude capture engage when they should [[25:23|AIH 1-19]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

A change or disruption of the navigation source may drop the autopilot to wings-level mode [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. On some autopilots, switching the HSI from GPS to VOR in NAV mode defaults lateral control to ROL until the pilot reengages NAV [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
Choose the level of automation for the job and change it as things change. One of the most common errors is failing to move to a lower level when the situation changes [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Know the disconnect procedures and where the checklists are; read the system documentation and AFM supplements [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].

body.p: In the annunciator strip, the green modes are engaged: heading, autopilot and altitude hold at 9,000 ft. The white LOC and GS are armed, waiting to capture [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. Teach learners to read that strip after every change, not the button they pressed.

callout.text: Plan the autopilot failure before you need it. Known before departure, a dead autopilot changes the risk picture; failing at a high-workload moment, it can turn into an emergency unless the pilot has decided in advance how to handle it [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

The RMH says pilots should train with automation under VFR with a qualified, knowledgeable instructor before IFR, and that a simulation device lets them repeat procedures under a simulated high workload [[30:52|RMH 7-3]] [[30:53|RMH 7-4]]. The PHAK recommends occasionally disengaging the automation to hand-fly [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]. Build both into your syllabus.

check.q: ATC unexpectedly cancels your learner's GPS route and gives vectors. What level of automation does the RMH example suggest?
check.a: Lower it: use basic autopilot modes that control heading and altitude, so the pilot can reprogram while the flight path stays under control [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

chunks.title: Distraction, priorities, disorientation and the EFB

body.p: Navigation equipment is a classic distraction. Programming is simple, but these devices tend to capture the pilot's attention and hold it for long periods, so the pilot should plan in advance when and where to program, and when not to [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]. When information exceeds what the pilot can process, the choice is to shed unimportant tasks or do everything poorly [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

head: Risk
What to teach and watch for
rows: Distractions
Teach the learner to divide attention between the distracting task and aircraft control; the AIH list includes having the learner determine a heading to an airport using a chart [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
Task prioritization

Load waypoints before departure and minimize head-down time with a sharp lookout [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]. Once airborne, budgeting time, prioritizing tasks or slowing down gives time to finish tasks without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Loss of situational awareness

Highly reliable automation breeds complacency, and a pilot may follow it even when common sense says otherwise; be especially alert with experienced learners on a flight review [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]. Following only the magenta line can lead into high terrain or prohibited airspace [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
Disorientation

If lost: climb (better radio, navigation and radar reception), use navigation radios or GPS to fix position, communicate with any facility, and in a threatening situation use 121.5 MHz and squawk 7700 [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

body.p: Spotting it in the learner. Humans perform poorly as passive monitors of a GPS or autopilot, and the more reliable the system the worse they watch it [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Glance at the learner's eyes: a long stare at one display suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Ask about other traffic and the aircraft's position on the chart, or create an imaginary problem with the navigation equipment, and point out when control or scanning suffers [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

head: EFB (R5): AC 91-78A says
Teaching point
rows: An EFB may replace paper if it replaces no required equipment, shows equivalent information, is current as verified by the pilot, and does not interfere with aircraft systems [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]]
The tablet replaces charts, never a required radio, and currency is the pilot's job.
In-flight use is the operator's and PIC's decision; no formal approval if the AC is followed [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.2]]
The learner owns the decision and its risk.
Assess workload, integration, display and lighting, shutdown and failures, placement and stowage [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]]
Brief where the tablet lives for takeoff and what happens when it dies or overheats.
Train on preflight checks, each function used, when not to use it, and cross-checking data entry and computed results [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.2]]
Have the learner check one computed number by hand each flight.

callout.text: The moving map is never meant to substitute for a VFR sectional [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]. FIS-B weather on the tablet does not replace a preflight briefing and should not be the only source of weather [[33:306|AIM 4-5-9]].

check.q: How can you tell in flight whether a learner is fixating on the GPS?
check.a: Watch where the learner looks: a long stare at one display suggests fixation; also ask about traffic and chart position to test situational awareness [[25:82|AIH 3-31]] [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

chunks.title: System limits and losing the signal

head: System
Limits (R3)
Signs of loss (R4)
What to do
rows: VOR
Line of sight; terrain blocks it; cone over the station [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]] [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]]
Flag, needle oscillation, missing or T-E-S-T identifier [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]] [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]
Climb, change navaid, use pilotage and dead reckoning [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]
DME
Slant range; groundspeed and time valid only flying directly to or from the station [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]]
No distance, or only the DME identifier [[33:73|AIM 1-1-7]]
Use cross radials or a time check [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]
NDB/ADF
Static from lightning; distant stations at night [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]]
No flag; noisy identifier with erratic needle [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]]
Monitor the identifier continuously [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]]
GPS (VFR)
No integrity standard or RAIM alerting; antenna placement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]]
Large position jump, wrong clock time, position error warnings, other pilots reporting problems [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]
Verify with conventional navaids, revert, and promptly tell ATC [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]

body.p: GPS loss reaches beyond the map. Jamming or spoofing can also cause unreliable terrain alerts, a wrong position on the moving map and EFB, and lost or wrong ADS-B output [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]]. RAIM is only partly effective against spoofing, so the pilot may see no warning and ATC may be the only one who notices [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. Surveillance is line of sight too: low altitude or antenna shielding can cost radar or ADS-B contact, and climbing helps [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]].

bullets: Before departure: know the risk areas, check NOTAMs, plan fuel contingencies, plan to use conventional navaids at the destination [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]].
The VOR MON keeps nearly continuous VOR coverage at 5,000 ft AGL outside the western mountains and a non-GPS approach airport within 100 NM [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]] [[33:70|AIM 1-1-3]].
If automation misbehaves, reduce the level of automation, fly manually and take time to sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

callout.text: Teaching signal loss: the AIH suggests focusing the learner's attention on an imaginary problem with the navigation equipment and watching whether control and scanning hold up [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]. Application: say 'Your GPS just failed' and let the learner find the position with VOR and the chart before you allow the map back.

check.q: Why might a spoofed GPS give no warning at all?
check.a: RAIM is only partly effective against spoofing, so the pilot may not see erroneous indications; ATC may be the only one to notice [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

body.p: Operations. Radar traffic information warns a pilot of targets close enough to the route to need attention; it never relieves the pilot of seeing and avoiding [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]]. Workload, radar limits, traffic volume and frequency congestion can stop it, and the controller's reason need not be given [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]] [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

head: K3 item
What to teach
rows: Equipment

Surveillance radar shows no altitude unless the aircraft has Mode C and the facility can display it [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]]. Facilities display primary and secondary radar and ADS-B; with primary radar out, only transponder or ADS-B aircraft appear [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].
Available services

Basic radar service at all commissioned facilities: safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring and sequencing where established [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]]. TRSA: separation of participating VFR from IFR and other participants, by 500 ft vertical, visual separation or target resolution; participation urged, not mandatory [[33:219|AIM 4-1-18]] [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]]. Class C adds IFR/VFR separation and VFR arrival sequencing; Class B adds separation based on IFR, VFR and/or weight [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]].
Traffic advisories

Given by 12-hour clock azimuth, distance in NM, direction of flight, and type and altitude if known [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]]. The controller sees only your track, so a crab angle shifts where the traffic really is [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15]].
Vectors and safety alerts

Vectors to VFR aircraft are advisory and never authorize breaking a regulation; tell ATC about weather ahead because controllers may not know if a vector leads into clouds [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]. VFR pilots with Mode C may request MSAW monitoring; after a safety alert, what to do is the pilot's decision [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]] [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16]].

body.p: Communication procedures (S5). Initial contact: facility name, full call sign, and the request, for example 'request VFR traffic advisories' [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]]. Arriving pilots give position, altitude, call sign, type, beacon code, destination and request traffic information [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]]. Departing VFR pilots ask ground control or clearance delivery on initial contact, with direction of flight [[33:219|AIM 4-1-18]]. Report your exact altitude to the nearest hundred feet on initial contact [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

bullets: 'Radar contact' means you are identified and radar flight following will be provided until radar service is terminated [[34:401|AIM PCG R-2]].
Answer traffic calls with 'traffic in sight' or 'negative contact'; negative contact may be followed by a request for help avoiding the traffic [[34:432|AIM PCG T-9]] [[34:385|AIM PCG N-2]].
Monitor the frequency at all times and advise ATC when changing VFR cruising altitude [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].
'Resume own navigation' after vectors means you are responsible for your own navigation again [[34:406|AIM PCG R-7]].

To leave, advise the controller before changing frequency, then squawk 1200 if applicable [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]]. Arriving VFR, service ends automatically on landing at a tower airport with basic radar service, or elsewhere when told to change to tower or advisory frequency [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]].

callout.text: These services do not relieve pilots of seeing and avoiding traffic, avoiding wake turbulence, keeping terrain and obstruction clearance, or staying in VFR weather minimums. If an assigned route, heading or altitude would compromise those, tell approach control and get a revised instruction [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]].

check.q: In a TRSA, approach assigns your VFR learner 3,500 ft. Leaving the TRSA you hear 'resume appropriate VFR altitudes.' What must the learner do?
check.a: Return to an altitude that conforms to 14 CFR 91.159 as soon as practicable [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]].

chunks.title: Transponder Modes A, C and S, and ADS-B

head: System
What it does
Teaching point
rows: Mode A
Replies with a four-digit code, one of 4,096 [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]] [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]]
VFR code 1200 unless ATC assigns another [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]]
Mode C
Adds pressure altitude in 100-foot increments [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215]]; encoders are preset to standard pressure and ATC applies the local setting [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]
Installed equipment must have been tested to report within 125 ft of the altimeter reference [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217]]
Mode S

Replies to Mode A interrogations with the ATC code and to Mode S interrogations per TSO-C112 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.215]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215]]; most Mode S units also report altitude [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]]
Mode S data link carries TIS traffic to equipped aircraft near Mode S radars [[33:297|AIM 4-5-6]] [[23:125|IFH 5-30]]
ADS-B Out
Broadcasts GNSS position about once a second on 1090ES or 978 MHz UAT; 1090ES is required at and above 18,000 ft [[33:300|AIM 4-5-7]] [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]]
If installed, transmit at all times unless ATC says otherwise [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225]]
ADS-B In
Receives other ADS-B traffic plus TIS-B traffic and FIS-B information [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]]
Advisory only; no avoidance maneuvers just because a target appears [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]]

bullets: Operate transponder and ADS-B in altitude reporting mode on any airport movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20]]. In controlled airspace an installed transponder must be on with Mode C [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215]].
Press IDENT only when ATC asks [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]. When changing codes, avoid passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700; never use 7777 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

'Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs by...' may mean a bad encoder or a wrong altimeter setting. A wrong setting does not change the transmitted altitude but makes you fly at the wrong true altitude [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].
Test and inspect the transponder within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]].

FLT ID must match the aircraft identification on the flight plan or a call sign mismatch can delay services [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]]. UAT anonymous mode is only for code 1200 with no ATC services; turn it off before requesting flight following [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]].
TIS-B shows only transponder-equipped aircraft, updates every 3 to 13 seconds, can show your own target or duplicate shadows, and gives no sign when you are outside coverage [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8]].

body.p: Where they are required: in general, Mode C and ADS-B Out in Class A, B and C, above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class B or C up to 10,000 ft MSL, in Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL in the 48 states and DC except at and below 2,500 ft AGL, and within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport below 10,000 ft MSL [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

callout.text: An unequipped airplane that ATC clears into ADS-B airspace: acknowledge and fly the clearance, but tell the controller you are not ADS-B equipped and have no authorization [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]]. A good scenario question for a learner flying an older trainer.

check.q: Approach gives your learner a new code, 7400, while she is squawking 0700 on a knob-type transponder. She reaches for the first knob. What do you teach?
check.a: Set the other digits first (0700 to 0400, then 7400) so she never passes through 7700; routine code changes should avoid 7500, 7600 and 7700, which cause false alarms at automated ground facilities [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: the lesson flow

body.p: The demonstration-performance method has four phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Telling-and-doing adds the key middle step where the learner tells and the instructor does [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

head: Phase
Navigation lesson example
rows: Explanation (ground)
Objective and completion standards; sketch orientation and the intercept; brief which systems will be 'failed'. Encourage questions before leaving the ground [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Instructor tells, instructor does
Tune, identify, check the flag, intercept and track while talking, in the same order you briefed. If the demo departs from the explanation, say so at once [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through the next intercept; misunderstandings get fixed before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner tells, learner does
The learner flies and thinks out loud, so you can tell a misconception from a motor-skill error [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Evaluation
Collaborative assessment: learner self-assessment first, then your detailed assessment and a discussion comparing them [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

bullets: Use scenarios. A good scenario has clear objectives, fits the learner and uses the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Application: a real diversion near your local Class C with flight following beats a canned VOR drill.
Integrate instruments and outside references from the start, so the learner keeps monitoring aircraft performance [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Keep see and avoid alive. Learners who think the instructor watches for traffic never build the habit, and flight instructors were aboard in 37 percent of the midair collisions in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Be clear about who is flying during head-down tasks; the preflight briefing should include the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: sequence the blocks from known to unknown. Raw VOR and the chart first, then the HSI picture, then GPS on the same route, then the autopilot coupled to it. Each new layer is checked against the one below it.

check.q: What two benefits does the AIH give for the 'learner tells, instructor does' step?
check.a: The learner, free of flying, organizes the steps and techniques; and the instructor can evaluate the learner's understanding before the learner performs [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Careless tuning and identification [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Learner flies a needle before the identifier is confirmed
Tune, identify by audio or decoded ID, flag clear, then set the course [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]
Turning the wrong way during orientation [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Turn toward the wrong side after centering the needle
Have the learner state position, not heading, before turning [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Not checking TO/FROM, reverse sensing [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Corrections drive the needle further off
Set the OBS to agree with the intended course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Overshooting and overcontrolling near the station [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]
S-turns across the radial close in
Lead the turn and use smaller corrections as the needle gets more sensitive [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]
Chasing the CDI (homing) [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]
Heading changes every time the needle moves
Bracket the wind: correct, then halve the correction [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Misreading station passage [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]
Calls passage while transmitting or at a mountain needle swing
Read the whole receiver and confirm with TO/FROM [[23:259|IFH 9-16]] [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]
Mode confusion [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Airplane wings level after a source change; learner does not notice
Read the annunciators after every entry and call out armed and engaged modes [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Programming in flight [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]]
Head down, altitude and heading drifting
Load routes on the ground; one entry at a time with eyes outside between [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]
Trusting GPS without a cross-check [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]
Cannot name a VOR radial or landmark that confirms the map
Make the learner confirm position by a second method each leg [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Poor radar service etiquette [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]]
Leaves the frequency or changes altitude without telling ATC
Advise before leaving, squawk 1200; report altitude changes [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]]
Looking for traffic off the nose while crabbing [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15]]
Learner cannot find called traffic
Adjust the clock position for the crab angle [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15]]

callout.text: When an error repeats, reteach it: demonstrate, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate by watching the performance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Your learner corrects toward the needle and it moves further away. What is the likely error and the fix?
check.a: Reverse sensing from an OBS set to the reciprocal of the course; set the OBS to agree with the intended course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: the NAVAID box, part by part

body.p: Teach the NAVAID box as a small data block read left to right: name, frequency, channel, identifier and Morse code. The box also carries extra marks: a star, an underline, an icon for automated weather, and a crosshatch [[2:14|Chart Users' Guide p 14]] [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]]. Students who tune the frequency and skip these marks miss important facts.

Three marks cause most misreads. A star before the frequency means the station operates less than continuously or on request, so it may be off when the student needs it. An underlined frequency means no voice on that frequency, so do not wait for a voice broadcast. A crosshatched box means the NAVAID is shut down; do not plan to use it [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]]. Make the student say each one out loud before using the station.

The circled A icon means an ASOS or AWOS is available at the site [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]] [[2:26|Chart Users' Guide p 26]]. A student who reads it as 'airport' will not tune the weather. Also point out the compass rose: it is a reference oriented to magnetic north, so radials read from it are magnetic, not true [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

The FSS and RCO boxes work the same way. Frequencies above a thin-line box are remoted to the NAVAID site, and the name below it is the FSS that provides the voice communications. A thin-line box with a name but no frequencies means no FSS frequency is available; check the Chart Supplement for the rest [[2:26|Chart Users' Guide p 26]].

Finish with the rule behind the boxes: for IFR use of a VOR, the check must be within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. The chart tells the student what the station is; the regulation tells him whether his own receiver is good to use.

scenario.title: The magenta-line pilot meets a GPS test NOTAM
scenario.setup: Your learner is a 70-hour private pilot who bought a glass-panel trainer with a WAAS navigator, autopilot, a single VOR receiver and UAT ADS-B. She has not used the VOR since her checkride. Tomorrow you fly a dual 110 NM cross-country past a Class C airport with flight following. A GPS interference test NOTAM covers the middle third of the route.

questions.q: On the ground, how do you find out whether she understands her navigation systems or only knows the button sequences?
questions.a: Ask questions the box cannot answer: where the airplane is relative to chart references, which side of a station she is on. Rote learning is repeating without understanding [[25:65|AIH 3-14]], and asking about position on the chart tests situational awareness [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

questions.q: What do you plan because of the GPS test NOTAM?
questions.a: Know the risk area, plan fuel contingencies and plan to use conventional navaids at the destination [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]]. Check the VOR receiver, for example at a VOT [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]], and draw the route on a sectional for pilotage.

questions.q: Before taxi she has the route loaded. What check do you teach?
questions.a: Compare every leg with a paper log of headings and distances, and if they disagree do not assume the computer is right [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. Load all waypoints on the ground, not in the air [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].

questions.q: She is about to call approach for flight following with UAT anonymous mode on. What do you coach?
questions.a: Turn anonymous mode off first; it is only for code 1200 with no ATC services [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]]. Then call with facility, full call sign and request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]], and report exact altitude to the nearest hundred feet [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

questions.q: In the test area the map jumps 4 NM and the coupled autopilot begins to turn. What should she do?
questions.a: Reduce the automation level, fly heading and altitude by hand or in basic modes [[30:51|RMH 7-2]], verify position with the VOR and pilotage, and promptly tell ATC if she needs help [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Expect ADS-B and the EFB map to be affected too [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]].

questions.q: How do you run the debrief?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then yours, then compare [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Grade automation management progressively from describe to practice to manage-decide over several flights [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

skills.do: Use an airborne electronic navigation system while simultaneously explaining it from the right seat. The ACS sets no numeric tolerance for this CFI element; the examiner looks for correct tuning and identification, a flag check, the right course and source, mode awareness on the autopilot, and an explanation a learner could follow (ACS AI.II.H.S1).
skills.practice: Talk through tune, identify, flag, set, and anticipate, act, verify [[30:51|RMH 7-2]] on every flight. Use your receiver's simulator mode [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] to rehearse the explanation.

skills.do: Determine the airplane's position with the navigation system and explain how: cross radials, radial and DME, or a time check, and confirm the GPS position by a second method (ACS AI.II.H.S2).
skills.practice: Fix position with two VORs and with a radial and DME [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]], then do an RMI or CDI time and distance check [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]] [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]] and compare.

skills.do: Intercept and track a given course, radial or bearing while explaining the intercept angle, the wind correction and why you are not homing (ACS AI.II.H.S3).
skills.practice: Use the IFH double-the-difference method [[23:257|IFH 9-14]] on several intercepts at different distances from the station, and practice explaining while you bracket the wind.

skills.do: Recognize and describe the indications of station or waypoint passage out loud as they happen, including fly-by versus fly-over behavior on GPS (ACS AI.II.H.S4).
skills.practice: Fly over a VOR and call each indication [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]; fly a GPS route with fly-by and fly-over waypoints and describe the turns [[33:110|AIM 1-2-1]].

skills.do: Use proper communication procedures with radar services: correct initial contact, exact altitude report, traffic replies, altitude change reports and leaving the frequency, and explain each to the examiner as a learner would hear it (ACS AI.II.H.S5).
skills.practice: Request VFR traffic advisories on every practice flight using the AIM format [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]] and close with the controller before changing frequency [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

quiz.q: In general, which ADS-B Out link does the AIM say an aircraft needs to fly at or above 18,000 ft?
options: 978 MHz UAT
Either UAT or 1090ES
A Mode S transponder only
quiz.why: ADS-B on 978 MHz is the Universal Access Transceiver (UAT), and on 1090 MHz it is 1090ES. In general, operators flying at 18,000 ft and above (Class A airspace) must have 1090ES equipment; those that do not fly above 18,000 ft may use either UAT or 1090ES [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].

quiz.q: Why must a pilot keep monitoring the identifier of an NDB?
options: NDB identifiers change at night
NDB signals are line of sight
The AIM requires a log entry for each NDB used
ADF receivers have no flag to warn of erroneous bearings
quiz.why: ADF receivers have no flag, so the pilot should continuously monitor the identification [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]].

quiz.q: Taxiing out at a towered airport, your learner leaves the transponder in standby until the runway. What does the AIM say?
options: Only ADS-B Out needs to be on during taxi; the transponder stays in standby until airborne
Standby is correct until takeoff clearance, so the ground radar is not cluttered by taxiing traffic
Altitude-reporting mode and ADS-B Out should be on any time the airplane is on the movement area
Standby is correct at towered airports, but altitude mode is needed while taxiing at nontowered ones
quiz.why: Operate the transponder in the altitude reporting mode, with ADS-B Out transmissions enabled, at all airports any time the aircraft is on any portion of the airport movement area, including all defined taxiways and runways [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20]].

quiz.q: Your learner plans to fly direct to a VOR from well inside its standard service volume, but a ridge lies between. What does the AIM say the SSV protects?
options: Signal strength, course quality and freedom from interference, but not blockage by terrain
Signal strength and course quality everywhere inside it, terrain included
Nothing at all for VFR pilots; SSVs apply only to published IFR routes
Reception at any altitude within 40 NM of the station, including the cone directly above it
quiz.why: The SSV is a three-dimensional volume in which the FAA ensures adequate signal strength and course quality, free from interference from other NAVAIDs, but that protection does not include blockage from terrain or obstructions, and a conical area directly above the NAVAID is generally not usable. The SSV is meant mainly for off-route navigation, such as proceeding direct to or from a VOR [[33:73|AIM 1-1-8]].

quiz.q: What does 'Anticipate' mean in the RMH's anticipate, act, verify steps?
options: Expect the autopilot to fail and keep a hand near the disconnect
Know what should happen before you push a button or turn a knob
Program the whole route before engine start so nothing is entered in flight
Predict ATC's next instruction and preload it before it is given
quiz.why: Anticipate means knowing what should happen before pushing a button or turning a knob [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

quiz.q: Which does the RMH call one of the most common automation errors?
options: Not moving to a lower level of automation as conditions change
Engaging the autopilot before trimming the airplane for the climb
Hand-flying so often that automation skills are never fully learned
Using the flight director alone without coupling the autopilot to it
quiz.why: One of the most common errors is failing to move to lower levels of automation suitable to a changing environment [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

quiz.q: How does the AIM describe the names of stand-alone VFR waypoints?
options: Five letters beginning with VW, pronounceable, so you can report them to ATC
Five letters beginning with VP, not pronounceable and not for ATC communications
Three letters and a number, the same format used for IFR fixes on the airways
Five letters beginning with VP, pronounceable, and used to report position to ATC
quiz.why: VFR waypoint names consist of five letters beginning with VP; they are not intended to be pronounceable and are not for use in ATC communications. Waypoints collocated with visual checkpoints are pronounceable from the checkpoint's name and may be used with ATC [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: Participating VFR aircraft in a TRSA are separated from IFR aircraft by which of these?
options: 500 ft vertical, visual separation or target resolution
1,000 ft vertical or 3 NM lateral, whichever the controller picks
Traffic advisories only, with separation given just to IFR aircraft
No separation; the TRSA gives only sequencing to the primary airport
quiz.why: TRSA service uses 500 ft vertical separation, visual separation or target resolution [[33:219|AIM 4-1-18]] [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]].

quiz.q: When should a VFR pilot press the transponder IDENT button?
options: Only when ATC requests it
When entering Class C
On every initial contact with approach or center
Whenever changing codes
quiz.why: Activate IDENT only when requested by ATC [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

quiz.q: Installed altitude reporting equipment must have been tested to report altitude within how many feet of the altimeter reference?
options: 50 ft
125 ft
200 ft
100 ft
quiz.why: 14 CFR 91.217 requires correspondence within 125 feet on a 95 percent probability basis [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217]].

quiz.q: A VOR box on the legend shows a star before the frequency. What does the star tell your student?
options: The station operates part-time or on request
The station is restricted to military aircraft
The station is temporarily shut down for repairs
The station has continuous weather broadcasts
quiz.why: The legend labels the star as 'operates less than continuous or on-request' [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

quiz.q: A student sees an underline under the frequency in an NDB box, as for MONTAGUE 404. What is the correct reading?
options: The station gives a continuous weather broadcast
The station is crosshatched and shut down
No voice on this frequency
The frequency is for emergencies only
quiz.why: The legend says the underline indicates no voice on this frequency [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

quiz.q: On the legend, the SALEM VOR-DME box is drawn with crosshatching. What do you teach your student to do?
options: Tune it, since crosshatching shows an ILS
Use it only during night flights
Treat it as shut down and not rely on it
Use it, but expect no DME distance readout
quiz.why: The legend states that crosshatch indicates shutdown status [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

quiz.q: A small 'WX CAM' symbol appears on the legend. What does it show?
options: A military weather observation unit
An off-airport weather camera location
A Class B airspace reporting point
A weather radar site for precipitation
quiz.why: The legend lists WX CAM under off-airport weather camera locations [[2:26|Chart Users' Guide p 26]].

quiz.q: Your IFR student's VOR was last checked 35 days ago, and the airplane is not maintained under an approved VOR procedure. May she use it for IFR flight today?
options: Yes, a VOR check is good for 60 days in IFR flight
Yes, if the error found was under 6 degrees at the check
No, the VOR check must be made within the last 30 days
No, a VOR check is only valid on the day of the flight
quiz.why: For IFR use of VOR, the equipment must be maintained under an approved procedure or have been checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your flight review client has 900 hours, flies his own glass airplane and follows the magenta line flawlessly. Which AIH warning applies most?
options: Watch closely for complacency; the AIH warns of it in experienced learners on flight reviews
Experienced pilots rarely need automation training, so spend the time on stick and rudder skills
Grade him only on the magenta line, since flawless tracking proves he manages the automation
Glass airplanes cannot be used for flight reviews, so he must review in a round-dial trainer
final_quiz.why: Highly reliable automation can induce complacency, and the AIH tells instructors to be especially alert to it in experienced learners on a flight review [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

final_quiz.q: A GPS outage is NOTAMed along your learner's VFR route in the eastern U.S. Her airplane also has a VOR receiver. What does the VOR MON give her?
options: GPS-independent position from ADS-B ground stations along each Victor airway
A VOR signal at any altitude above 1,000 ft AGL and a MON airport with an ILS within 25 NM
Nothing for VFR pilots; the MON keeps VORs only for IFR aircraft and their filed alternates
Nearly continuous VOR reception at 5,000 ft AGL and an airport with a non-GPS approach within 100 NM
final_quiz.why: The VOR MON retains enough VORs, with larger service volumes, for nearly continuous VOR reception at 5,000 ft AGL, and keeps an aircraft within 100 NM of an airport with an instrument approach that does not depend on GPS. In a planned outage, pilots may fly through it using the MON [[33:70|AIM 1-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: Planning a VFR route through a mountain pass, your learner wants to fly direct from one VFR waypoint entry point to the next. What do you teach?
options: Only with flight following, since ATC then provides terrain clearance through the pass
That is the published path through the pass, so it is safe in any weather
Only with a current database, because the waypoints then define a protected route
The points do not make a path through the pass; choosing the route is the PIC's job
final_quiz.why: Mountain pass entry points are for convenience and do not create a path through the pass [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: On flight following, your learner climbs from 4,500 to 6,500 ft to clear a ridge without saying anything to approach. What do you teach?
options: Nothing; VFR pilots on flight following may change altitude freely without telling ATC
She should have squawked 1200 before climbing, then called approach again at the new altitude
Tell the controller when changing VFR cruising altitude, and keep monitoring the frequency
She needed an ATC clearance for the climb, since flight following makes her a controlled flight
final_quiz.why: Pilots receiving VFR radar advisory service should monitor the frequency and inform the controller when changing VFR cruising altitude; to leave the service, advise the controller before changing frequency and then squawk 1200 if applicable [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

final_quiz.q: You are training a learner in an older trainer with no ADS-B Out. ATC turns you onto a heading that will cross ADS-B rule airspace. What should she say and do?
options: Refuse the heading, because entering ADS-B airspace without ADS-B Out is never allowed
Acknowledge and fly it, but advise she is not ADS-B equipped and has no authorization
Fly it without comment; ATC's instruction counts as authorization to enter
Squawk 7600 and fly the heading, so ATC knows she lacks the equipment
final_quiz.why: The AIM says to acknowledge and execute the clearance but advise that the aircraft is not ADS-B equipped and has no authorization; ATC then continues or modifies it [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]].

final_quiz.q: After a series of vectors around traffic, approach says 'resume own navigation.' Your learner keeps flying the last heading. What does the phrase mean?
options: Keep the last heading until told otherwise
Radar service is terminated and she should squawk 1200
Squawk 1200
The pilot is again responsible for navigation
final_quiz.why: 'Resume own navigation' advises the pilot to resume his or her own navigational responsibility after vectors [[34:406|AIM PCG R-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is departing VFR from a towered airport with radar sequencing service and wants traffic advisories. When and how should she ask?
options: Call approach after takeoff on the sectional frequency
Ask tower on the runway, after the takeoff clearance, giving her destination
File a VFR flight plan, because departing traffic advisories are given only to aircraft on one
Tell ground control or clearance delivery on initial contact, with direction of flight
final_quiz.why: Departing VFR pilots are encouraged to request radar traffic information from ground control or clearance delivery on initial contact, with the proposed direction of flight [[33:219|AIM 4-1-18]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is inbound VFR to an airport the Chart Supplement lists for VFR sequencing service. When does the AIM say to call approach, and what will approach assume?
options: At the Class C outer area edge, 20 NM out; she must ask for sequencing by name
About 10 miles out; approach then assumes she wants only traffic advisories
About 25 miles out; on initial contact approach assumes she wants sequencing
About 5 miles out, after first calling tower, which hands her off to approach
final_quiz.why: Pilots of arriving VFR aircraft should initiate radio contact with approach control about 25 miles from an airport where sequencing service is provided, and on initial contact approach control will assume that sequencing service is requested [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]].

final_quiz.q: Over mountains, your learner flies the direct magenta line on the moving map and never looks at the sectional. What does the PHAK warn about that strategy?
options: Nothing, as long as the database is current, since the moving map already draws the terrain and the airspace along the line
Only that the line can drift, so recheck it against the GPS track every 10 minutes
Only that the map may not show TFRs, which are the one thing a sectional covers better
Following only the magenta line can lead into high terrain or prohibited airspace, or leave her lost if the map fails
final_quiz.why: A pilot whose navigation strategy consists solely of following the magenta line on the moving map can easily fly into geographic or regulatory disaster if the straight-line GPS course goes through high terrain or prohibited airspace, or if the moving map display fails [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. The moving map is never meant to substitute for a VFR sectional [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner hears a 'low altitude alert' from approach while VFR in hilly terrain. Who decides the response?
options: The pilot alone
The controller, who will issue a mandatory climb
The tower
The pilot and controller decide jointly
final_quiz.why: Once a safety alert is issued, it is solely the pilot's prerogative to decide what action, if any, to take [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]].

final_quiz.q: A flight school operator asks what to assess before adopting tablets in its trainers. Which list matches AC 91-78A?
options: Price, brand, battery size and whether the app is on an FAA-approved software list
Workload, integration, display and lighting, shutdown and failures, placement and stowage
Only the FAA approval number of the app and the date of its last database update
Wi-Fi coverage at the airport, cellular data in flight and the tablet's screen size and weight
final_quiz.why: AC 91-78A lists workload, integration, display and lighting, system shutdown and failures, and placement and stowage [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].

final_quiz.q: Flying a VOR at 9,000 ft AGL in rugged terrain, your learner sees a brief needle oscillation but the flag still reads TO. What do you teach?
options: That is station passage; turn to the outbound course now and set the new radial
Some mountain stations show a brief swing like station approach; use the TO/FROM flag for passage
The VOR is out of service, so report it to Flight Service and switch to pilotage
Switch to GPS and ignore the VOR, since mountain VORs are not usable above 5,000 ft AGL
final_quiz.why: At a few stations, usually in mountains, a brief oscillation resembles approaching the station; use the TO/FROM indicator to determine positive passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner on flight following sees a target on the ADS-B display closing from the right in clear weather but has not spotted it. What is correct?
options: Turn away based on the display, since ADS-B position is accurate to a few feet
Ignore the display; ADS-B In targets are unreliable and not worth her time in clear weather
Use it only to help find the traffic; no avoidance maneuver is authorized just because a target shows
Ask ATC for an IFR clearance, so the controller must separate her from the target
final_quiz.why: ADS-B traffic displays are only to help visual acquisition; no avoidance maneuvers are authorized as a direct result of a displayed target [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]].

final_quiz.q: A VORTAC box on the legend has a small circle with an A at its upper right. What does your student gain from it?
options: An ASOS or AWOS is available at the site
An approach lighting system is installed
The station operates on request only
The station is an NDB
final_quiz.why: The legend labels the circled A as ASOS/AWOS [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]]; automated weather services are shown by the same symbol [[2:26|Chart Users' Guide p 26]].

final_quiz.q: On the legend, HANCOCK RCO shows 122.525 and 123.65 above the box and 'GREEN BAY' below it. What does 'GREEN BAY' tell the student?
options: The FSS that provides voice service on those frequencies
The location of the remote receiver site, 20 NM away
The name of the Class C airport it serves
The nearest towered airport that also uses those frequencies
final_quiz.why: Frequencies above the box are remoted to the NAVAID site, and the controlling FSS name below it shows the FSS providing voice communications [[2:26|Chart Users' Guide p 26]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's transponder was last tested and inspected 26 calendar months ago. What does the regulation say?
options: It may not be used until tested within the preceding 24 calendar months
It may still be used if the Mode C altitude reads true
It may still be used until 36 calendar months after the test
It may still be used for VFR flights, but not for IFR flights
final_quiz.why: No one may use an ATC transponder unless it has been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]].

takeaways: Teach the concept before the knobs: a learner who can say where the airplane is relative to the station and the chart is navigating; one who repeats key presses is at the rote level.
Tune, identify, flag clear, then set the course; the VOR ignores heading, and position, not heading, decides which way to turn.
VOR checks are required only for IFR (30 days, 4 and 6 degree limits, a signed entry); for VFR use the IFR limits as a guide.
VFR GPS has no RAIM alerting and no integrity standard; load the route on the ground, keep the database current near critical airspace, and always cross-check.
Anticipate, act, verify: read the mode annunciators after every entry and step down the automation when things change.
Radar services are advisory and workload-permitting; they never relieve see and avoid, wake avoidance, terrain clearance or VFR minimums.
Teach with telling-and-doing and real local scenarios, then debrief with the learner's self-assessment first.
cfi_notes: The sources disagree on the crab-angle traffic picture: PHAK Figure 14-44 says aircraft A sees the 12 o'clock traffic at 1 o'clock [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]], while AIM FIG 4-1-1 says 2 o'clock for the same drawing [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15]]. Teach the AIM, and the real lesson: the controller sees only track.

PHAK Figure 14-43 describes 'SQUAWK (number)' as operating on a code in Mode A/3 [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]]; the AIM phraseology says operate on the code with altitude reporting enabled [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20]]. Teach the AIM wording.

IFH 9-16 says the 30-day VOR check needs 'an appropriate endorsement' and tells you to tune 'the VOT frequency 108.0 MHz' [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. 14 CFR 91.171 asks only that the person checking enter the date, place and bearing error and sign the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171]]. The AIM just says to tune in the VOT frequency, and gives 108.0 MHz as the frequency normally approved for repair station test signals [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]] [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. Teach the CFR wording, and have learners look up each VOT's frequency instead of assuming 108.0.
PHAK 16-32 says many VFR receivers and all hand-held units lack RAIM alerting [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]; the AIM says VFR panel-mount and hand-held units have none [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. Teach the AIM.

The PHAK's tracking example starts with a 10 degree wind correction [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]], while the IFH says to begin with a 20 degree correction [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Both are starting points to bracket from; pick one and teach it consistently.

The sources are silent on how to simulate a GPS or VOR failure in flight. The AIH only suggests an imaginary problem with the navigation equipment [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]; brief any simulated failure on the ground and never let it hide a real one.
Examiners for this Task will likely play a learner who has a misconception, such as reading the TO/FROM flag as 'toward the nose'. Rehearse the correction with the IFH picture [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
Flight following is a gift for teaching radio work: the AIH says scenarios should exploit the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Use the nearest approach control on every cross-country lesson.

Brief the learner that a simulated failure may come at any time and who flies while the learner is head down; the AIH wants a clear understanding of who has the controls at all times [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
gaps: How a specific navigator, autopilot or EFB app behaves (mode names, source-change logic, CDI scaling annunciations): only its AFM supplement and pilot guide, as the ACS note says.
Mode S is described here only through 14 CFR 91.215 (TSO-C112 replies) and its TIS data link role; the handbooks give no plain explanation of selective interrogation.
No source gives a required VOR check interval or tolerance for VFR; the PHAK only suggests the IFR limits [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].
The AIM says there is no indication when an aircraft is inside or outside TIS-B coverage [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8]], and no source says how to judge it in flight.
AC 91-78A lists EFB training topics but gives no syllabus or completion standard; the CFI builds that.

Full needle deflection means 12 degrees or more off course
Pointer shows the course to the selected navaid; no course to set

No warning flag, so keep monitoring the station identifier

activities.intro: Tap an item, then tap whether 14 CFR requires it or the AIM or PHAK only recommends it.

activities.title: Work the position numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: With the RMI pointer on the wingtip, a 10 degree bearing change takes 90 seconds. How many minutes to the station?
items.why: Seconds divided by degrees of bearing change gives minutes to the station [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]: 90 / 10 = 9 minutes.

items.q: Same check, groundspeed 120 knots. How far to the station?
items.why: Distance is NM per minute times minutes [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]: 120 knots = 2 NM per minute; 2 x 9 = 18 NM.

items.q: Using the CDI method, the OBS is moved 10 degrees and the needle takes 2.5 minutes to center again. Time to the station?
items.why: Time = 60 x minutes flown / degrees of bearing change [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]: 60 x 2.5 / 10 = 15 minutes.

items.q: Same check at a TAS of 110 knots. Distance to the station?
items.why: Distance = TAS x minutes flown / degrees of bearing change [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]: 110 x 2.5 / 10 = 27.5 NM.

items.q: Your learner is 75 NM from the VOR and the CDI shows she is 3 degrees off the selected radial. About how many NM is she off course?
items.why: Each degree is 1 NM wide at 60 NM and the width is proportional to distance [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]: 75 / 60 = 1.25 NM per degree; 3 x 1.25 = 3.75 NM.

items.q: Your learner crosses directly over a VORTAC and the DME reads 1.3 NM. About how high above the station is the airplane, in feet?
items.why: DME is slant range; directly over a VORTAC at 6,076 ft AGL it shows about 1.0 NM [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]] [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]]. 1.3 x 6,076 = 7,898.8, about 7,900 ft.

activities.title: Read the crab, find the traffic
activities.intro: The controller sees only each airplane's track. Drag each description to its numbered pin on the airplane it describes.

pins.label: Eastbound, nose crabbed left into a north wind
Westbound, nose crabbed right into a north wind
Northbound, crabbed left into a west wind: traffic called at 2 o'clock appears at 3 o'clock
No crab needed (headwind): traffic called at 11 o'clock is where it was called

activities.title: Dual cross-country with a GPS-trusting learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI on a dual VFR cross-country in a glass-panel trainer with GPS, autopilot and one VOR. Your learner is flying.

steps.s: Before taxi, the learner has the route loaded and wants to go. What do you have her do?
options: Trust the loaded route and add any extra waypoints in flight once she is level and settled
Confirm the database cycle is current and then trust the route, since the computer does the math
Load the route again from scratch and accept whatever the second entry shows without comparing
Compare each leg with a paper log of headings and distances and recheck if they differ
steps.why: Verify programming against a paper log before departure and do not assume the computer is right if they differ [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

steps.s: En route she is head down adding a waypoint, and the airplane has drifted 200 ft high. What do you do?
options: Fix the altitude yourself without comment, then let her go back to finishing the waypoint entry
Let her finish the entry since altitude is not critical VFR, and mention the drift in the debrief
Take the tablet away and have her keep it stowed for the rest of the flight to avoid distraction
Point out that control is slipping, have her fly first, then make one entry at a time
steps.why: Point out when too much attention leaves aircraft control or scanning [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]; minimize head-down time and avoid programming in flight [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]] [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].

steps.s: You announce, 'Your GPS has just failed.' What should she do first?
options: Switch to the tablet's GPS map and stop cross-checking the chart or the VOR for the rest of the leg
Call 121.5 and declare an emergency before doing anything else
Keep flying, then fix position with the VOR, the chart and landmarks
Turn back immediately and land at the departure airport
steps.why: Use VOR to back up GPS [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]] and integrate pilotage and dead reckoning [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. An imaginary equipment problem is the AIH's suggested test [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

steps.s: Approaching her destination's CTAF, she starts to switch frequencies while still on flight following. What do you coach?
options: Advise the controller before changing frequency, then squawk 1200 if applicable
Stay with approach until you are on the ground, since leaving the frequency early cancels the service
Squawk 7600 as soon as she leaves the frequency so the controller knows she is on her own
Just switch to CTAF and let ATC notice the transponder code change on their own scope
steps.why: When advisory service is no longer desired, advise the controller before changing frequency, then change to 1200 if applicable [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

steps.s: On the return leg she tracks inbound to a VOR. The needle starts to swing, then the flag flips from TO to FROM and stays there. What do you want to hear and see?
options: Nothing yet; wait for the needle to center again and the flag to settle before reacting
A callout of station passage, then the turn to the outbound heading and the new course set
A report to ATC that the VOR is unreliable, with a request for vectors to the destination
A switch to GPS right away because the VOR has failed, then ignoring the needle
steps.why: A fluctuating needle that settles with the TO/FROM flag changing to FROM is station passage [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]]; callouts, even single pilot, keep situational awareness [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

activities.title: True or false: radar services
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A controller must tell you why traffic advisories cannot be provided.
cards.why: False. The reason is not subject to question and need not be communicated [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

cards.s: VFR radar advisory service includes vectors away from traffic only if you ask.
cards.why: True. It does not include vectors away from conflicting traffic unless requested [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

cards.s: Participation in TRSA service is mandatory for VFR pilots.
cards.why: False. Participation is urged but not mandatory [[33:219|AIM 4-1-18]].

cards.s: Class C service separates IFR from VFR aircraft.
cards.why: True. Class C service adds approved separation between IFR and VFR aircraft [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]].

cards.s: During a radar outage you no longer need a clearance to enter Class B airspace.
cards.why: False. Absence of radar does not negate the Class B clearance requirement [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18]].

cards.s: With the primary radar out, aircraft without a transponder or ADS-B may not show on the controller's display.
cards.why: True. Only aircraft with transponders and ADS-B in use are depicted then [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]].

activities.title: Transponder and ADS-B, ramp to ramp
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the AIM's transponder and ADS-B steps for one flight in order, then tap Check.
steps: Pushback or taxi-out: select altitude reporting and enable ADS-B
Taking the active runway: select TA or TA/RA, if TCAS equipped
In controlled airspace: assigned code, altitude reporting enabled
Leaving the runway after landing: deselect TA or TA/RA, keep altitude reporting on
At the parking spot: select STBY or OFF
